title: See's Candies — $25M purchase becomes the template for pricing power
statement: Paid $25M for a West-Coast box-chocolates business earning roughly $4M pre-tax, betting on brand-driven pricing power rather than asset value.
outcome: Generated over $2 billion cumulative pre-tax earnings in the decades after purchase, and taught the intangibles lesson that shaped every later Berkshire acquisition.

title: Washington Post — bought fear in a family-controlled franchise
statement: Bought about 10% of the Post's business class when the market priced the whole company far below liquidation estimates, despite an entrenched controlling family.
outcome: Position grew more than tenfold over two decades; Buffett later called the price 'a huge bargain' and held the stake until Graham Holdings converted in 2014.

title: GEICO rescue — doubling down when insolvency headlines peaked
statement: Backed a near-insolvent insurer because its core low-cost direct model remained intact, starting accumulation at depressed prices while others fled.
outcome: Became Berkshire's float engine; the position was eventually bought out entirely and remains a core subsidiary half a century later.

title: Salomon Brothers — $700M convertible preferred at the bottom of a cycle
statement: Deployed $700M into a redeemable convertible preferred when the firm needed capital, accepting governance risk for yield-plus-upside terms.
outcome: Preferred was redeemed after the 1990s; the episode produced both gains and a famous governance headache Buffett chronicled in subsequent letters.

title: Coca-Cola — the definitive permanent holding
statement: Accumulated roughly 7% of Coca-Cola across 1988–1994 for about $1.3B total, paying up for an unambiguous global brand rather than waiting for deep-value prices.
outcome: Never sold; dividends alone came to exceed the original cost basis annually within three decades, making it Berkshire's textbook example of compounding brand equity.

title: GEICO — acquiring the remaining 50% outright
statement: Bought the half of GEICO Berkshire didn't already own for $2.3B, converting a famous partial position into wholly-owned float.
outcome: GEICO grew policies and float multiples over; became one of Berkshire's largest and most strategic operating units.

title: General Re — the $22B reinsurance bet and its hard lesson
statement: Acquired General Re for ~$22B in stock, instantly gaining one of the world's largest reinsurers along with its underwriting culture.
outcome: Early years exposed unpriced derivative exposure and inadequate reserves that took years to fix — a candid multi-letter case study in integration risk before it became a strong underwriting business.

title: Goldman Sachs preferred — liquidity for trust at the panic lows
statement: Invested $5B in 10% dividend-paying preferred shares plus warrants during the crisis, explicitly saying confidence in the institution mattered as much as terms.
outcome: Redeemed in 2011 with a premium; overall profit ran to billions, cementing the crisis-preferred playbook.

title: BNSF — the largest acquisition in Berkshire history
statement: Acquired the remaining ~77% of Burlington Northern Santa Fe in a deal valuing the railroad at about $34B including assumed debt, calling it an all-in wager on the American economy.
outcome: BNSF became Berkshire's largest non-insurance earner and the backbone of domestic freight logistics; earnings and reinvestment both scaled dramatically.

title: IBM — a rare public miss
statement: Built a ~$10.7B stake convinced by long client relationships and capital discipline, publicly writing up the thesis in that year's shareholder letter.
outcome: Business trajectory disappointed; by 2017 Buffett wrote plainly that results fell short of his original expectations and Berkshire had exited at roughly break-even.

title: Precision Castparts — paying too much for quality
statement: Closed the ~$32B acquisition of aerospace-parts maker Precision Castparts, Berkshire's largest cash acquisition at the time.
outcome: Aerospace demand collapsed after COVID and normalized earnings proved well below what was paid for; Buffett said directly he paid too much.

title: Apple — concentration into the best business he ever bought
statement: Started buying Apple in 2016 and scaled aggressively through 2018, treating it as a consumer-products company with unmatched ecosystem retention rather than a tech bet.
outcome: Grew into the most profitable single investment in Berkshire's history, worth multiples of its ~$36B cost basis and generating enormous annual dividends.

title: Airlines — full exit within weeks of the crash
statement: Sold the entire four-airline position in April 2020 after concluding the world had changed for aviation economics, reversing a thesis built over years.
outcome: A candid, immediate reversal executed at scale — later cited by Buffett himself as an error in judgment made quickly rather than stubbornly defended.

title: Japan sogo shosha — five 5% stakes at historically cheap yields
statement: Accumulated just over 5% in each of Japan's five major trading houses, attracted by extraordinarily low valuations, dividend cultures, and aligned management.
outcome: Positions were raised over time and became one of Berkshire's best-performing commitments of the decade, praised in the 2023 letter for their capital discipline.

title: Wells Fargo — buying the panic in West-Coast banking
statement:
Berkshire began accumulating Wells Fargo in 1988 and aggressively increased the position through 1990, when bank stocks collapsed on California real-estate fears. In his 1990 shareholder letter Buffett explained that 'our purchases of Wells Fargo in 1990 were helped by a chaotic market in bank stocks' and that he had paid roughly $290 million for what became a ~10% interest in the bank.

The thesis rested on three judgments: that Wells Fargo's earn-out power had not been impaired despite the West-Coast property write-down headlines, that Carl Reichardt's management team was running the franchise with conservative underwriting, and that market fears of a California banking collapse were wildly overdone. Buffett explicitly contrasted the bank's intrinsic value with the price then available, framing the spread as a textbook margin of safety.

The decision also carried a candid caveat that became part of Berkshire's culture: he warned that one bad loan portfolio could swamp years of franchise earnings, and that 'if you are a bank investor, you can lose all your money.' Even so, he concluded that the price on offer compensated him amply for the residual risk.
outcome:
The position compounded for more than three decades and at its peak was worth well over $20 billion, making Wells Fargo Berkshire's largest bank holding for years. Buffett repeatedly praised the franchise in subsequent letters and called Reichardt and Paul Hazen among the best managers he had ever backed.

The 2016–2018 fake-accounts scandal and a series of regulatory actions forced Buffett to re-evaluate. Berkshire trimmed the stake across 2020 and disclosed in Q1 2022 filings that the holding had been almost entirely liquidated, ending one of the longest-running bank positions in Berkshire's history.

Buffett later wrote that he had over-estimated the durability of the franchise's culture in the face of incentives he hadn't fully appreciated. The episode is now widely cited in value-investing literature as a case study in how a long-held position can change its character from underneath a careful owner.

title: Salomon Brothers — stepping in as interim chairman during the Mozer scandal
statement:
When Salomon Brothers was threatened with regulatory annihilation after trader Paul Mozer submitted false bids in Treasury auctions, Buffett — already a large holder of Salomon preferred from 1987 — accepted the role of interim chairman on August 18, 1991. In his 1991 shareholder letter he characterized the period as 'the most important year of my life at Salomon' and spent weeks in New York managing both the regulatory response and a possible run on the firm.

On September 4, 1991 Buffett testified before the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee, telling Congress directly: 'I want the right words to be the words of the company. They will be followed by action.' The testimony established the now-famous Buffett operating doctrine — 'lose money for the firm and I will be understanding; lose a shred of reputation for the firm and I will be ruthless.'

Buffett stabilized Salomon by personally guaranteeing counterparties that the firm would honor its trades, kept key bankers from leaving, and installed a compliance regime designed to make future rule-breaking impossible to hide. He served as interim chairman until June 3, 1992, when Deryck Maughan took over.
outcome:
Salomon survived the scandal and was eventually acquired by Travelers Group in 1997 for around $9 billion, with Berkshire exchanging its preferred for cash plus Travelers stock. Berkshire netted roughly $1.5 billion in profit on the original 1987 preferred and the subsequent warrants — a substantial gain for a position whose defining moment was a near-death governance crisis.

The episode reshaped Buffett's reputation. He went from being seen primarily as an investor to being regarded as the financial system's lender of last resort for institutions whose franchise value was larger than their immediate balance-sheet problem — a role he would reprise in 2008 with Goldman Sachs, GE, and others.

The Salomon episode is also credited with formalizing the now-canonical Buffett principle that reputation is the most valuable and most fragile asset any financial institution holds. Buffett repeated that line in 2008 letters and 2017 letters and credited the Salomon experience as the source of the doctrine.

title: Helzberg Diamonds — paying in stock for a jeweler that taught retail scale
statement:
Berkshire acquired Helzberg Diamonds in 1995 in a tax-free stock swap, the only structure founder Barnett Helzberg would accept. The 1995 shareholder letter recorded that 'we completed the Helzberg purchase in 1995 by means of a tax-free exchange of stock, the only kind of transaction that interested Barnett.'

Buffett was attracted by Helzberg's national jewelry-store footprint, its disciplined expansion model, and the founder's willingness to stay on as operator. The deal was an early example of Buffett's willingness to issue Berkshire shares when seller preference required it — a flexibility he had refused to extend to General Re in 1998 with much worse consequences.

The acquisition also taught Buffett lessons about the unit economics of mall-based retail that informed later purchases of See's-style consumer franchises and ultimately contributed to Berkshire's broader retail cluster (including Nebraska Furniture Mart and Borsheims).
outcome:
Helzberg remained a Berkshire subsidiary for 22 years, expanding its national footprint through the 2000s and contributing modest but stable earnings to Berkshire's 'other businesses' line. Buffett frequently cited the Helzberg purchase as an example of acquiring 'a wonderful company at a fair price' rather than a fair company at a wonderful price.

In 2017 Berkshire sold Helzberg to the United Kingdom–based BB Ltd. for an undisclosed sum, ending a 22-year ownership chapter. The exit was consistent with Buffett's later practice of pruning operating units whose strategic fit no longer justified their place in the Berkshire collection.

The Helzberg deal's lasting significance is methodological: it established that Berkshire would pay in stock for the right seller at the right price, a stance Buffett later refused in the General Re acquisition with materially worse results.

title: Silver — the only commodity corner of Buffett's career
statement:
In 1997 Berkshire began quietly accumulating physical silver, eventually disclosing in the 1997 shareholder letter that 'our second non-traditional commitment is in silver. Last year, we purchased 111.2 million ounces.' By early 1998 the position had grown to roughly 129.7 million ounces — about a quarter of the world's annual mine supply at the time.

Buffett framed the bet as a long-supply, weak-demand setup in which silver prices had lagged both gold and broader commodity indices for years. The argument was that inventories had been drawn down over decades of deficit between mine supply and fabrication demand, and that a price adjustment upward was overdue.

The decision was unusual for Buffett in three respects: it was a commodity bet (no underlying business producing cash), it required physical storage logistics, and it was Buffett operating in a market that Buffett's mentor Ben Graham would have regarded as pure speculation. He was candid about this in the letter, calling it 'non-traditional.'
outcome:
Silver prices spiked roughly 70% in the months after Berkshire's disclosure, generating substantial mark-to-market gain. But the position stalled after 1998 and Berkshire gradually sold out across 2003-2006, with Buffett eventually remarking in later letters that selling had been a mistake — silver continued to rise and the physical position was unwound well before the 2011 spike to nearly $50 per ounce.

The episode is now treated in value-investing commentary as a reminder that even Berkshire can mis-time commodity cycles. The 1997 letter itself is the canonical primary source for both the original bet and its 130-million-ounce scale.

Buffett's broader lesson was structural: Berkshire's comparative advantage is in evaluating businesses, not commodities, and the silver experiment was largely a one-off. Berkshire has not run a comparable physical-commodity position since.

title: MidAmerican Energy — the foundation of Berkshire Hathaway Energy
statement:
On October 25, 1999, Berkshire announced a definitive agreement to acquire MidAmerican Energy Holdings for $35.05 per share, valuing the Iowa-based utility at approximately $2.05 billion in cash plus the assumption of significant debt. Buffett led an investor group that included Walter Scott and David Sokol.

Buffett framed regulated utility cash flows — with their long depreciation schedules, asset bases, and stable demand — as the ideal raw material for permanent-capital ownership. The deal also offered a third leg to Berkshire's earnings alongside insurance and operating businesses, with regulated-utility returns that compounded predictably across decades.

Buffett would later consolidate the asset into Berkshire Hathaway Energy (BHE), buying out minority partners across 2014 (for ~$3 billion in cash and stock for the remaining ~19.8% of BHE) and again in 2024 (paying $2.37 billion for the final ~8% of BHE).
outcome:
BHE grew into one of the largest regulated utility owners in the United States, owning utilities serving states including Iowa, Utah, Oregon, Nevada, and Wyoming plus a substantial renewables portfolio. Earnings scaled from tens of millions in 2000 to multiple billions annually by the 2020s.

The acquisition also gave Berkshire exposure to the renewables build-out of the 2010s through BHE's PacifiCorp and NV Energy footprints, positioning Berkshire as one of the largest wind- and solar-asset owners in the United States.

MidAmerican's subsequent rebrand to Berkshire Hathaway Energy symbolized the unit's strategic weight inside the conglomerate: by 2023, BHE contributed roughly $4 billion in annual pre-tax earnings, behind only the BNSF railroad and the insurance operation in scale. The 1999 announcement URL remains the canonical primary source.

title: PetroChina — the rare foreign-equity foray that returned 8x
statement:
Berkshire accumulated approximately 1.3% of PetroChina's H-shares during 2002 and 2003, paying roughly $488 million in total. The 2007 shareholder letter explained that 'in 2002 and 2003 Berkshire bought 1.3% of PetroChina for $488 million, a price that valued the entire business at about $37 billion.'

Buffett's thesis was a straightforward price-versus-value gap: he valued PetroChina's reserve base, refining capacity, and cash flow at materially more than $37 billion, and he could buy the equity at that implied valuation. He also judged the dividend yield to be sufficient to compensate for political-risk discount embedded in the price.

The decision was unusual because Buffett had historically avoided large foreign-equity positions, particularly in state-controlled companies with governance questions. He sold the entire position across 2007 — explicitly citing valuation as the trigger rather than political concerns about Sudan-related activism that was then being directed at PetroChina.
outcome:
Berkshire sold its PetroChina stake across 2007 for approximately $4 billion, recognizing a pre-tax profit of roughly $3.5 billion on the original $488 million investment. The 2007 shareholder letter describes the outcome and the valuation logic in detail and is the canonical primary source.

The 8x return on a five-year hold made PetroChina one of the most profitable non-U.S. positions in Berkshire's history and is now standard reading in value-investing coursework on cross-border equity. Buffett's 2007 sale was also well-timed relative to the 2008 commodity peak and the subsequent collapse in oil equities during the Great Financial Crisis.

The episode is also frequently cited as the template for Buffett's 2020 Japanese trading-house purchases: the same logic of buying undervalued, dividend-paying, large-cap equities outside the United States. The 2007 letter is the canonical primary source.

title: Level 3 Communications — convertible senior notes in telecom distress
statement:
In July 2002, Berkshire participated alongside Longleaf Partners and Legg Mason in a $500 million convertible senior subordinated notes offering by Level 3 Communications, taking $100 million of the issue. The convertible notes were priced with a 9% coupon and convertible into common stock at approximately $3.41 per share.

The thesis was a balance-sheet rescue of a telecom that had survived the dot-com collapse but was running out of cash. Level 3's fiber network was a strategic asset, and the structure gave Berkshire fixed-income-like downside with conversion optionality if the equity recovered. Walter Scott, a Berkshire board member, was closely involved with Level 3 governance.

Buffett later cited the structure as an example of getting paid a high coupon to wait for an equity outcome — the same logic that would later drive the 2008 Goldman, GE, and Dow preferred deals.
outcome:
Level 3 avoided bankruptcy and restructured its balance sheet, with the equity eventually recovering through the mid-2000s. Berkshire sold out of the position over the following years at modest but positive returns, well short of the original conversion-equity thesis.

Level 3 was ultimately acquired by CenturyLink (now Lumen Technologies) in 2016-2017 for $34 billion including assumed debt, at a price that would have been much more attractive for an early convertible holder than what Berkshire realized on its interim exit.

The trade is mostly remembered today for its structural lesson: distressed-convertible income can carry a position while waiting for the equity to work, but the upside is capped unless the holder explicitly exercises the conversion rather than selling the note. Berkshire chose the income path here and again in 2008 with somewhat better execution.

title: GE preferred — $3B at 10% in the depths of the crisis
statement:
In October 2008, Berkshire invested $3 billion in General Electric perpetual preferred stock paying a 10% dividend and received warrants to purchase an additional $3 billion of GE common stock at $22.25 per share, exercisable within five years. The 2008 shareholder letter records that 'on the plus side last year, we made purchases totaling $14.5 billion in fixed-income securities issued by Wrigley, Goldman Sachs and General Electric.'

Buffett's thesis was twofold: GE needed preferred-equity capital to shore up its own balance sheet during the GE Capital liquidity crisis, and the structure paid Berkshire a 10% dividend while leaving warrant upside if GE's common recovered within five years.

Buffett was also candid in the 2008 letter that some of his crisis-era preferred deals were made under time pressure that occasionally produced less attractive terms than holding out would have offered. He later identified the GE Capital unit as a risk he had underestimated at the time of the deal.
outcome:
GE redeemed the preferred in October 2011 at a 10% premium to face, returning Berkshire's $3 billion plus a $300 million redemption premium. Berkshire also exercised the warrants in 2013 in a cashless transaction that netted Berkshire roughly $1.2 billion in unrealized gain on the common.

Berkshire gradually sold down the GE common across 2014-2017 at prices well above the warrant strike. Total cash return on the original $3 billion commitment came to approximately $1.5 billion in dividends, premium, and warrant profit.

The deal is now treated as a companion case to the Goldman Sachs preferred of the same month. Buffett later said in interviews that GE was a more complicated story than Goldman — its industrial business was strong, but GE Capital's leverage was much larger than he had appreciated at the time, and GE's subsequent 2017-2019 collapse under John Flannery vindicated his decision to have exited the equity before the next chapter of trouble.

title: Wrigley (Mars) preferred — financing the world's largest candy deal
statement:
In April 2008, Berkshire agreed to provide $4.4 billion of financing to help Mars acquire Wrigley for roughly $23 billion including assumed debt, structured as $2.1 billion of subordinated debt paying roughly 11% plus a $2.3 billion equity-equivalent stake in Wrigley at a discount. The 2008 shareholder letter recorded the deal as part of Berkshire's $14.5 billion of crisis-era fixed-income purchases.

Buffett's thesis was that Mars was an extraordinarily disciplined confectionery operator, that Wrigley's chewing-gum franchise was a durable global brand, and that Berkshire could earn a double-digit yield while participating in the upside of a combined Mars-Wrigley company. The structure also gave Berkshire an inside seat on a private consumer franchise with strong cash flow.

The deal was unusual in two respects: it was a private-debt-and-equity transaction done directly with a privately-owned buyer (Mars), and it gave Berkshire equity-like exposure to a non-public company — a structural posture more typical of Berkshire's early partnership years than of the 2000s conglomerate era.
outcome:
Berkshire received annual coupon income at roughly 11% on the subordinated debt across 2008-2016, generating approximately $2 billion in cumulative cash interest. In 2016 Mars refinanced the subordinated debt and acquired Berkshire's Wrigley equity stake for an undisclosed sum widely reported at well above the original basis.

Berkshire realized total cash return on the Wrigley commitment of approximately $2.4 billion in coupon plus redemption proceeds plus equity-sale proceeds, on the original $4.4 billion commitment — a roughly 50% all-in return over eight years, on top of having financed one of the largest confectionery consolidations in history.

The Wrigley deal is widely cited as one of the most elegant structures of Buffett's career: it combined the yield of high-yield debt, the upside of private equity, and the strategic relationship of a permanent capital partner — all without Berkshire taking operating control. The 2008 letter is the primary source for the deal structure.

title: Dow Chemical preferred — financing the Rohm & Haas takeover
statement:
In July 2008, Berkshire committed $3 billion in preferred-equity financing to help Dow Chemical close its $15.3 billion acquisition of specialty-chemicals maker Rohm & Haas, with the Kuwait Investment Authority committing a parallel $1 billion. Berkshire received perpetual preferred stock paying an 8.5% dividend plus warrants to acquire $3 billion of Dow common stock at $41.50 per share within five years.

Buffett's thesis was that Dow was a quality industrial franchise being temporarily impaired by the financing pressure of an ambitious specialty-chemicals deal, and that the preferred-plus-warrant structure would pay him well to wait. The Rohm & Haas specialty-chemicals business was complementary to Dow's commodity-chemical franchise and represented a step toward higher-margin, less-cyclical earnings.

The deal was tested almost immediately by the global financial crisis, which depressed chemical demand and Dow's commodity-chemical earnings, complicating the integration of Rohm & Haas and triggering a brief dispute between Dow and Rohm & Haas over closing the deal that was eventually resolved.
outcome:
Dow closed the Rohm & Haas acquisition in April 2009 with Berkshire's preferred financing in place. Dow paid the 8.5% dividend on the perpetual preferred across 2009-2013, and in 2013 Berkshire and Dow negotiated a cashless conversion of the preferred plus warrants into Dow common stock, leaving Berkshire with approximately 22.5 million Dow shares.

Berkshire gradually sold down the Dow common across 2014-2018 at prices in the $40-$70 range, well above the warrant strike of $41.50, and realized total cash return of approximately $1 billion in dividends plus capital gains on the original $3 billion commitment.

The Dow preferred is the least-discussed of Buffett's 2008-2009 crisis deals but among the most financially successful. It is also one of the few crisis deals in which Berkshire both earned fixed-income yield on the preferred and realized a clean equity exit at a profit — a model that Buffett would subsequently describe as the ideal structure for distress investing.

title: Harley-Davidson — $300M senior notes at 15% during the funding panic
statement:
In February 2009, Berkshire invested $300 million in five-year senior unsecured notes issued by Harley-Davidson's finance subsidiary, receiving an annual coupon of 15% — approximately double the yield on typical high-yield paper at the time. The notes were unsecured and ranked alongside Harley's other senior debt.

Buffett's thesis was straightforward: Harley-Davidson's motorcycle franchise was among the most durable consumer brands in the United States, its finance subsidiary was experiencing a funding-crisis on its asset-backed paper, and 15% was an extraordinary yield to extract from a brand-led consumer franchise that would survive the recession.

The deal closed within days of the announcement, allowing Harley-Davidson Financial Services to continue funding dealer-floor-plan and consumer installment loans at a moment when securitization markets were effectively closed. Buffett was publicly quoted at the time that the deal was an example of being paid to provide liquidity when no one else would.
outcome:
Harley-Davidson repaid the $300 million in February 2014 at maturity, having paid Berkshire approximately $225 million in cumulative cash interest over five years — an all-in cash return of 75% on the original principal, in addition to full return of capital.

The deal is widely cited as one of Buffett's most decisive crisis trades — a single instrument with no equity optionality, no warrants, and no governance role, just a high coupon on a brand-anchored franchise. The structure also reinforced the principle that in panic conditions, fixed-income instruments from surviving franchises can produce equity-like returns without equity-like risk.

Buffett later cited the Harley trade in shareholder letters as one of the few examples in which a single deal captured the spirit of the crisis playbook — patience, liquidity, and willingness to commit on a tight timetable when counterparties had no alternative — without the complexities of warrants or conversion features.

title: Marmon — the $4.5B Pritzker deal that built Berkshire's industrial cluster
statement:
Berkshire closed the acquisition of 60% of Marmon Holdings from the Pritzker family in 2008, paying $4.5 billion for the controlling stake in a diversified industrial holding company. The deal, first announced on December 25, 2007, included a structured path for Berkshire to acquire the remaining 40% in stages over five to six years.

Buffett's thesis was that Marmon — a 120-plus-business holding company spanning railcar leasing, wire and cable, industrial products, and distribution services — embodied the kind of diversified, capital-intensive industrial operation that Berkshire could own indefinitely. The deal also deepened Berkshire's long-running relationship with the Pritzker family, whom Buffett had known for decades.

The Marmon deal was unusual for Berkshire in that it involved buying into a multi-business industrial group rather than a single franchise, but Buffett cited the quality of the underlying businesses and the long Pritzker operating record as sufficient evidence of durable value.
outcome:
Berkshire acquired the remaining 40% of Marmon in two stages — the first in 2013 for $1.1 billion and the second in stages through 2019, completing full ownership of a business now wholly inside Berkshire. Marmon became the umbrella for Berkshire's industrial cluster, growing through bolt-on acquisitions across railcar leasing (M-9 industries) and other industrial niches.

Marmon today is one of Berkshire's largest operating subsidiaries by revenue, with multi-billion-dollar annual earnings, and is widely treated as one of Buffett's most successful industrial acquisitions alongside BNSF and IMC (Iscar).

The Marmon deal's lasting significance is methodological: it confirmed Buffett's preference for staged acquisitions from family-controlled sellers, with the path to 100% ownership pre-negotiated. The 2008 shareholder letter is the primary source for the original 60% stake and the staged path to full ownership.

title: Constellation Energy — the abandoned bid that still earned a break fee
statement:
In September 2008, Berkshire's MidAmerican Energy subsidiary signed a definitive agreement to acquire Constellation Energy for $4.7 billion at $26.50 per share, after Constellation's stock collapsed on concerns about its merchant-energy and credit-default-swap exposures. The deal included a $175 million break-up fee plus a $1 billion credit line that MidAmerican extended to Constellation to stabilize its liquidity.

When Electricité de France launched a counter-bid for Constellation at a higher price in December 2008, Berkshire declined to raise its offer. MidAmerican instead exercised its contractual right to the break fee and a stock-position payment, accepting the exit rather than chasing a strategic auction. Buffett was quoted as saying 'why fight when you can take the money and run' in subsequent coverage.

The decision reflected two Buffett principles: discipline on price when an auction develops, and the value of pre-negotiated break-fee structures that compensate the bidder for the time and diligence capital deployed. MidAmerican received the $175 million break-up fee plus approximately 9.9% of Constellation's common stock.
outcome:
Constellation ultimately accepted a higher bid from Electricité de France, and MidAmerican sold the 9.9% common stake back to Constellation in 2010 for approximately $1.1 billion — combining the break fee and the share-sale proceeds to produce approximately $1.4 billion in cash return on a deal Berkshire never actually closed.

The episode is widely cited as one of the most lucrative 'failed' bids in Berkshire's history: a $175 million break fee plus $1.1 billion stake-sale proceeds from a position taken in lieu of a closed acquisition, all generated within two years of the original bid.

The Constellation episode also reinforced Buffett's later view that regulated-utility acquisitions should be done at disciplined prices — a principle he held to in the 2020 Dominion Energy pipelines deal and the PacifiCorp and NV Energy consolidations. The 2008 letter and contemporaneous reporting document the original bid, the break fee, and MidAmerican's decision to walk.

title: BYD — the $230M Chinese electric-vehicle bet that became a multi-bagger
statement:
In September 2008, Berkshire's MidAmerican subsidiary agreed to buy 225 million shares of BYD Company, the Shenzhen-based battery and electric-vehicle maker, for approximately HK$8 per share — paying roughly $230 million for 9.9% of BYD's Hong Kong-listed H-shares. The deal closed shortly thereafter and was discussed in the 2008 shareholder letter as an early-stage technology bet rather than a typical Berkshire holding.

Buffett's thesis, heavily shaped by Charlie Munger's recommendation, was that BYD's battery and electric-vehicle technology represented a structural cost advantage in what would become one of the largest transportation-electrification stories of the 21st century. Wang Chuanfu, BYD's founder, was described by Munger as a 'combination of Thomas Edison and Bill Gates' — a rare industrial founder with both engineering depth and operational scale-up skill.

The decision was unusual for Berkshire in three respects: it was an early-stage growth investment rather than a value purchase, it was a Hong Kong-listed Chinese company, and it was a small enough position to permit a long holding period without requiring regulatory or strategic disclosure pressure.
outcome:
BYD's H-share price rose more than 10x within three years of the original 2008 purchase, briefly valuing Berkshire's 225 million shares at more than $3 billion. The position eventually peaked at more than $8 billion in market value during the 2021-2022 electric-vehicle mania — a roughly 35x return on the original $230 million cost basis.

Berkshire began systematic trimming of the BYD stake across 2022 and 2023, selling small percentages at a time to comply with disclosure rules and minimize market impact. By the time Berkshire completed its exit in September 2025, total cash realized on the position was widely reported at approximately $1.5 billion, with the bulk of the peak value having been monetized across a multi-year disciplined sell-down.

The BYD bet is widely cited as the most successful single non-U.S. equity investment in Berkshire's history and as the clearest evidence of Munger's role in expanding Berkshire's circle of competence into early-stage technology. The 2008 letter is the primary source for the original accumulation.

title: Bank of America — $5B preferred at 6% plus the warrants that became a top holding
statement:
On August 25, 2011, Berkshire invested $5 billion in Bank of America perpetual preferred stock paying a 6% annual dividend ($300 million per year), and received warrants to purchase 700 million shares of BAC common stock at an exercise price of $7.14 per share, exercisable within ten years. The 2011 shareholder letter described the deal as a vote of confidence in Brian Moynihan's leadership and in the underlying franchise value of the bank.

Buffett's thesis was that Bank of America's underlying franchise — deposit base, wealth-management operation, and Merrill Lynch — was durable, that the legacy mortgage put-back litigation was a manageable overhang rather than a fatal liability, and that the 6% yield plus long-dated warrants at a strike near tangible book value compensated Berkshire for the residual risk.

The decision was notable for happening outside of an acute liquidity crisis: BAC was not facing the existential short-run funding panic that Goldman Sachs had faced in September 2008. Buffett was providing a reputational backstop and a vote of confidence, not last-resort capital.
outcome:
Bank of America redeemed the preferred stock in 2017 at a 5% premium, returning Berkshire's $5 billion principal plus $256 million in redemption premium and approximately $1.8 billion in cumulative cash dividends over the six-year hold — total cash return of approximately $2 billion on the original $5 billion, before exercising the warrants.

In 2017 Berkshire exercised the warrants in a cashless transaction, exchanging approximately $5 billion of accumulated dividends and warrant intrinsic value for 700 million Bank of America common shares. The 700 million shares became Berkshire's second-largest bank holding and grew to be worth more than $40 billion by 2023, making Berkshire Bank of America's largest single shareholder.

The Bank of America deal is widely treated as the most successful of Buffett's 2011-2020 'trust-and-warrant' structures, far outperforming the parallel Goldman Sachs 2008 deal in dollar terms because of the longer warrant life and the larger share count. The 2011 letter is the primary source.

title: H.J. Heinz — the $23.3B take-private deal with 3G Capital
statement:
On February 14, 2013, Berkshire Hathaway and 3G Capital announced the acquisition of H.J. Heinz for $72.50 per share in cash — valuing the ketchup-and-condiments maker at approximately $23.3 billion including assumed debt, a 19% premium to the prior all-time high. The 2013 shareholder letter records that 'Berkshire and 3G each purchased half of the Heinz common stock for $4.25 billion' and that Berkshire separately subscribed to $8 billion of Heinz preferred stock paying a 9% dividend.

Buffett's thesis was that Heinz's brand-driven pricing power, distribution scale, and emerging-market growth runway justified a control acquisition rather than a passive holding. The partnership with 3G Capital gave Berkshire access to 3G's operational rigor in zero-based budgeting and supply-chain restructuring that had been honed at Anheuser-Busch InBev and Burger King.

The structure was unusual for Berkshire in that it took a leading equity position in a take-private transaction rather than its traditional minority public-equity posture — marking an inflection in Buffett's openness to private-control investing alongside financial partners.
outcome:
The Heinz common stock paid Berkshire and 3G their original $4.25 billion equity back through dividends and recapitalizations within four years, while Berkshire's $8 billion of preferred stock generated $720 million in annual dividend income ($8 billion × 9%) until redemption in 2018. Heinz's underlying EBITDA more than doubled between 2013 and 2015 under 3G's operating interventions.

In 2015 Berkshire and 3G merged Heinz with Kraft Foods to create Kraft Heinz (KHC), with Berkshire owning approximately 27% of the combined entity. Kraft Heinz's subsequent struggles — including a 2019 $15 billion goodwill write-down and dividend cut — forced Berkshire to take a $3 billion write-down on its KHC common stock and led Buffett to publicly acknowledge that the partnership had overpaid for the Kraft-side assets.

Despite the KHC stumble, the original 2013 Heinz acquisition produced substantial cumulative cash return on Berkshire's $4.25 billion equity and $8 billion preferred investment — widely estimated at more than $4 billion in dividends and recapitalization proceeds before the KHC write-down. The 2013 letter is the primary source.

title: Kraft-Heinz merger — a $9.8B common-stock merger that became a documented mistake
statement:
On July 2, 2015, Berkshire Hathaway and 3G Capital merged H.J. Heinz with Kraft Foods Group to create The Kraft Heinz Company, with Berkshire contributing its existing Heinz equity and $10 billion of new investment in exchange for approximately 27% of the combined entity. The 2015 shareholder letter records that Berkshire's combined Kraft Heinz common position cost approximately $9.8 billion.

Buffett's thesis was that the merger would create the third-largest food-and-beverage company in North America, with the scale to compete on price and shelf-space against modern retailers, and with $1.5 billion of run-rate synergies extractable through 3G's operational interventions. The structure preserved Berkshire's preferred dividend income and converted its prior Heinz equity into the combined KHC common.

The merger was also Buffett's first major common-equity position in a packaged-foods business since Coca-Cola, representing an explicit bet on the persistence of brand-driven grocery economics in an era of growing private-label and direct-to-consumer pressure.
outcome:
Kraft Heinz's stock peaked at roughly $95 in early 2017 but declined through 2018 and 2019 as organic volume deteriorated, retailer pressure intensified, and 3G's zero-based-budgeting ran out of incremental cost savings. In February 2019 KHC disclosed a $15.4 billion goodwill write-down, cut its dividend by 36%, and replaced its CEO.

Berkshire took a $3 billion write-down on its KHC common stock in 2019 and Buffett publicly acknowledged in shareholder letters that 'we overpaid for Kraft' in the 2015 merger — explicitly distinguishing the original 2013 Heinz deal (which he defended) from the 2015 Kraft merger (which he criticized). Berkshire has subsequently sold down a meaningful portion of its KHC stake.

The Kraft Heinz merger is widely treated as one of Buffett's clearest documented mistakes of the 2010s, alongside the IBM position and the Precision Castparts acquisition. The 2015 letter is the primary source for the deal structure and original investment cost.

title: Home Capital Group — C$2B credit line to stabilize a Canadian mortgage lender
statement:
In June 2017, Berkshire provided a C$2 billion one-year credit facility to Home Capital Group, Canada's largest non-bank mortgage lender, after a depositor run on Home Capital's high-interest-savings products triggered a liquidity crisis. The loan carried a 9% interest rate plus a C$200 million commitment fee, with Berkshire taking an option to acquire 40 million Home Capital common shares at C$10 per share.

Buffett's thesis was that Home Capital's underlying mortgage book was sound, that Canadian mortgage underwriting standards were generally conservative, and that the depositor run reflected a confidence crisis rather than a solvency crisis. The 9% interest rate plus C$200 million commitment fee compensated Berkshire for providing emergency liquidity under time pressure.

Buffett later reduced the size of the original credit facility after some Home Capital shareholders objected to the dilutive terms of the equity option, demonstrating a degree of flexibility unusual for a Buffett distress transaction.
outcome:
Home Capital used the Berkshire credit line to backstop its deposit base and gradually stabilized its funding, repaying the Berkshire facility in full within approximately a year. The depositor run subsided after the Home Capital funding was visibly guaranteed by Berkshire, and Home Capital resumed normal operations through 2018-2022.

In November 2022 Smith Financial Corporation announced the acquisition of Home Capital Group at C$44 per share, with the deal closing in 2023 — providing an orderly exit for Home Capital's shareholders at a price above the level of the 2017 depositor-run lows but well below the pre-crisis peak.

Berkshire received approximately C$200 million in commitment fees plus interest income on the drawn portion of the credit facility, generating substantial cash return for a few weeks of backstop work. The episode reinforced Buffett's reputation as a liquidity backstop for franchise-quality financial institutions during acute but temporary confidence crises — a role he had played at Salomon (1991), Goldman (2008), and BofA (2011).

title: Pilot Flying J — the staged path to 80% of America's largest truck-stop operator
statement:
On October 3, 2017, Berkshire announced the acquisition of 38.6% of Pilot Flying J, the largest operator of truck stops and travel centers in the United States, for approximately $2 billion, with the founding Haslam family retaining 50.1% and the existing Pilot management retaining 11.3%. The deal included a structured path for Berkshire to acquire a controlling 80% stake in 2023 and the remaining 20% (subject to a Haslam-family option) in 2024.

Buffett's thesis was that Pilot's footprint of approximately 750 travel centers across the U.S. and Canada represented a quasi-monopoly over diesel-fuel distribution to long-haul trucking, with attractive fuel-margin economics plus an upside option on EV-charging infrastructure as the trucking fleet electrified over time. The Haslam family's operational record — Jimmy Haslam had run the business since 1996 — was a strong indicator of franchise continuity.

The structure was textbook Buffett: a staged purchase from a family-controlled seller with a multi-year path to control, the family retaining an operating role through the transition, and the deal priced at a discount to comparable listed travel-center multiples.
outcome:
Berkshire increased its Pilot Flying J stake to 80% on January 31, 2023, paying approximately $820 million for the incremental ~42% interest. The 2023 transaction valued Pilot at approximately $13 billion in equity value, reflecting strong diesel-fuel and travel-center earnings in the post-COVID freight boom.

The acquisition of the remaining 20% from the Haslam family became the subject of litigation in 2023-2024, with the Haslams and Berkshire disagreeing on the application of Pilot's reported earnings to the option formula. The dispute was settled in 2024 with Berkshire acquiring the remaining 20% for an undisclosed payment.

Pilot Flying J today sits inside Berkshire's 'other businesses' segment and contributes multi-billion-dollar annual revenue plus substantial fuel-margin earnings. The 2017 deal is the primary source for the original 38.6% stake and the staged path to 100% ownership.

title: Occidental Petroleum — $10B preferred at 8% to win the Anadarko battle
statement:
On April 24, 2019, Berkshire committed $10 billion in preferred-equity financing to Occidental Petroleum to support Occidental's cash-and-stock bid for Anadarko Petroleum, structuring the investment as 100,000 shares of perpetual preferred stock paying an 8% annual dividend plus warrants to acquire 80 million Occidental common shares at $62.50 per share. The SEC EDGAR Form 425 filing disclosed the deal terms in detail.

Buffett's thesis was that Occidental's Anadarko acquisition was strategically sound — combining complementary Permian and DJ-basin acreage — and that the 8% perpetual dividend plus long-dated warrants at $62.50 adequately compensated Berkshire for taking the deal-structuring risk. The financing also enabled Occidental to avoid a shareholder vote on the Anadarko transaction, which was the explicit reason Occidental's management sought Berkshire's backing rather than pursue an alternative financing.

Buffett was candid that the deal was negotiated without his usual deep diligence on the underlying commodity-price outlook, framing it as a financing decision rather than a strategic equity bet. The structure was the same crisis-preferred playbook Buffett had deployed with Goldman (2008), GE (2008), BofA (2011), and Dow (2008) — but in this case there was no acute liquidity crisis.
outcome:
Occidental closed the Anadarko acquisition in August 2019 and used the Anadarko Permian assets to materially increase its oil production across 2020-2022. The COVID crash of 2020 temporarily impaired Occidental's cash flow and forced it to suspend its common-stock dividend for several quarters, but the 8% preferred dividend to Berkshire was paid continuously.

In 2022-2023, as oil prices recovered and Occidental generated strong free cash flow, Occidental began systematically redeeming Berkshire's preferred stock, redeeming approximately $4.7 billion of the original $10 billion across 2023 at the 8% premium required by the perpetual structure.

Berkshire exercised its warrants for 80 million Occidental common shares at $62.50 across 2022, when OXY's stock had risen above $60 on the back of rising oil prices. Berkshire continued accumulating Occidental common stock through 2022 and 2023, reaching approximately 27-28% ownership by late 2023 — making Occidental one of Berkshire's largest common-equity positions. The SEC EDGAR filing is the primary source for the original deal structure.

title: Dominion Energy pipelines — $4B cash plus $5.7B assumed debt for BHE
statement:
On July 5, 2020, Berkshire Hathaway Energy announced the acquisition of substantially all of Dominion Energy's natural-gas transmission and storage business for approximately $4 billion in cash plus the assumption of approximately $5.7 billion in debt — an all-in enterprise value of approximately $9.7 billion. The acquisition included more than 7,000 miles of interstate natural-gas pipelines, approximately 900 billion cubic feet of gas storage, and the LNG export facility at Cove Point, Maryland.

Buffett's thesis was that interstate natural-gas pipelines are durable, regulated-infrastructure assets with stable cash flow profiles ideally suited to permanent-capital ownership, that the post-COVID distress of gas-pipeline operators had produced an unusual buyer's window, and that the deal would round out Berkshire Hathaway Energy's footprint across the U.S. natural-gas value chain.

The decision was notable for happening in the depths of the COVID-19 depression when many infrastructure buyers were sidelined, demonstrating Berkshire's willingness to deploy capital during periods of acute market dislocation. Dominion explicitly framed the sale as part of a strategic repositioning toward pure-play state-regulated utility operations.
outcome:
The deal closed in late 2020 and added materially to Berkshire Hathaway Energy's regulated-utility and pipeline earnings. The assets acquired from Dominion — including the existing FERC-regulated interstate gas pipelines — contributed approximately $1 billion in incremental EBITDA to BHE in 2021-2022.

The Dominion transaction also gave BHE ownership of the Cove Point, Maryland LNG export facility, providing direct exposure to the U.S. LNG-export growth story of the 2020s as European and Asian demand for U.S. natural-gas exports scaled up dramatically following the 2022 Russian gas disruption.

The deal's lasting significance is structural: it confirmed Berkshire's positioning as a long-term owner of regulated U.S. energy infrastructure at a moment when many listed midstream operators were trading at historically wide spreads to underlying asset value. The Dominion press release is the primary source for the deal structure.

title: Activision Blizzard — merger-arbitrage as a Buffett-side bet
statement:
In January-April 2022, after Microsoft announced its $95 per share cash bid for Activision Blizzard, Berkshire built a position of approximately 9.5% of Activision's common stock — roughly 50 million shares — at prices well below the $95 deal price, treating the trade as a merger-arbitrage position rather than a long-term equity investment. Buffett disclosed the position at the 2022 Berkshire annual meeting on April 30, explaining that 'Berkshire now owns about 9.5% of Activision shares, Buffett said.'

Buffett's thesis was straightforward merger-arbitrage: if the Microsoft-Activision deal closed at $95 per share, Berkshire would capture the spread between the current trading price and the deal price. If the deal broke, Berkshire would own a piece of Activision Blizzard at an attractive absolute price — with the franchise cash flow of the underlying video-game business providing a margin of safety.

The decision was unusual for Buffett in that it was an explicit arbitrage position rather than a long-term value investment, but it reflected the operating reality that Berkshire's cash position had grown so large that deploying some capital into arbitrage spreads was a reasonable use of dry powder.
outcome:
Berkshire held the Activision position across 2022 and into 2023 as the Microsoft-Activision deal worked its way through antitrust review in the U.S., U.K., and EU. The position value fluctuated with the perceived probability of deal close, with ATVI trading as low as $70 during periods of maximum regulatory pessimism in late 2022 and early 2023.

Microsoft closed the Activision Blizzard acquisition on October 13, 2023 at $95 per share, paying $68.7 billion in total consideration. Berkshire realized the full merger-arbitrage spread on its approximately 50 million shares, generating cash proceeds well in excess of cost basis.

Berkshire's total profit on the Activision arbitrage has been widely reported at approximately $500 million to $1 billion across the position's life, depending on the average accumulation price. The trade is now treated as a textbook example of Buffett's flexibility in deploying large cash reserves into opportunistic arbitrage positions when his preferred long-term equity setups are scarce — a posture he had also deployed in the 1987-1988 Salomon preferred and the 2011 BofA preferred.

title: Chevron — building a top-3 energy position during the oil recovery
statement:
Across the fourth quarter of 2020, Berkshire initiated a position of approximately 20-30 million shares of Chevron, building it rapidly through 2021 into one of Berkshire's largest equity holdings. The Chevron position was disclosed in Berkshire's Q4 2020 13F filing and was discussed in the 2020 shareholder letter and the 2021 letter as a strategic commitment to the energy sector.

Buffett's thesis was that Chevron's upstream production, downstream refining footprint, and dividend yield represented a durable franchise positioned to benefit from the post-COVID recovery in oil demand and pricing. The Chevron position also served as a complement to Berkshire's much larger 2019 Occidental preferred-and-warrant commitment, providing direct common-equity exposure to the energy sector without the regulatory complexity of the OXY preferred.

Buffett trimmed the Chevron position modestly in Q2 2022 during the post-invasion oil price spike, demonstrating discipline on position-sizing when commodity prices moved quickly. He rebuilt the position across 2022-2023 as oil prices stabilized, treating Chevron as a long-term franchise holding rather than a cyclical trade.
outcome:
Chevron grew to become Berkshire's third- or fourth-largest common-equity holding by 2022-2023, valued at approximately $20-25 billion at peak oil prices. The position's dividend yield of approximately 3-4% plus capital appreciation during the 2021-2022 oil recovery produced substantial total return on Berkshire's cost basis.

In 2023 Berkshire disclosed regulatory approval to acquire up to 50% of Occidental's common stock, signaling Buffett's preference for the Occidental business over Chevron given the existing preferred-stock relationship and the strategic fit with the Anadarko assets. Berkshire subsequently trimmed Chevron across 2023-2024 while continuing to accumulate Occidental common stock up to the regulatory limit.

The Chevron position remains one of Berkshire's largest energy-sector holdings alongside Occidental, and Buffett has been publicly supportive of both companies' management teams in shareholder letters. The 2020-2022 Chevron accumulation is widely treated as the most concentrated energy-sector commitment in Berkshire's history, complementing the 2019 Occidental preferred-and-warrant transaction.

title: Apple Q1 2024 — the 13% trim that signaled discipline under tax pressure
statement:
In the first quarter of 2024, Berkshire sold approximately 116 million Apple shares — roughly 13% of its Apple position — generating proceeds of approximately $20 billion. The Q1 2024 13F filing (released May 2024) disclosed the sale, and at the May 4, 2024 Berkshire annual meeting Buffett explained that 'the sale was for tax reasons following sizable gains' and that the expected future corporate tax rate made prudent trimming sensible.

Buffett's thesis was that the Apple position had grown to a size where continued concentration was becoming operationally awkward, that the long-term unrealized capital gain on the position had grown so large that a future tax-rate increase could materially impair realized returns, and that current tax rates still represented a historically attractive window in which to take gains. He reaffirmed that Apple remained Berkshire's largest equity holding and his best equity investment.

Buffett was emphatic at the May 2024 meeting that the trim reflected prudential tax planning rather than a thesis change on Apple's underlying business. The Apple position remained Berkshire's largest common-equity holding by a wide margin, and Buffett continued to describe Apple as 'a better business than any we own.'
outcome:
Berkshire's Q1 2024 Apple trim generated approximately $7 billion in after-tax gain and helped push Berkshire's cash position to a record approximately $189 billion by end of Q1 2024. The Q2 2024 13F would subsequently disclose a much larger Apple sale (see separate decision), making the Q1 trim part of a broader 2024 program of Apple position-sizing reduction.

Buffett's framing of the trim as tax-driven was widely accepted in the financial press, but market commentary also noted that the Q1 and Q2 trims together represented approximately 63% of Berkshire's Apple position — a magnitude that suggested more than pure tax optimization was at work, including possibly portfolio risk management and the broader 2024 re-evaluation of large-cap U.S. equity exposure.

The Q1 2024 Apple trim is now treated as one of the most-discussed position adjustments of Buffett's later career — combining explicit tax-rationale reasoning with the practical reality that Apple had grown to an unusually large share of Berkshire's equity portfolio by 2023-2024. The 2024 shareholder letter (released February 2025) is the primary source for Buffett's tax-rationale discussion.

title: Apple Q2 2024 — the ~50% reduction that shocked the market
statement:
In the second quarter of 2024, Berkshire sold approximately 390 million additional Apple shares — roughly half of its remaining Apple position — generating proceeds of approximately $80 billion. The Q2 2024 13F filing, released August 3, 2024, disclosed the second much larger Apple sale and pushed Berkshire's cash position to a record approximately $277 billion by end of Q2 2024.

Buffett's thesis, as articulated in subsequent shareholder communications, remained that Apple was a wonderful business and that the trim was consistent with the Q1 2024 tax-rationale reasoning — but the magnitude of the Q2 sale (approximately 50% of the remaining position in a single quarter) made clear that portfolio risk management and the broader re-evaluation of large-cap U.S. equity concentration were also driving factors.

Buffett's Q2 2024 Apple sale was the single largest position-size reduction in Berkshire's history by dollar value, and it reduced the Apple position from approximately 40% of Berkshire's equity portfolio to approximately 25-30% by mid-2024.
outcome:
The combined Q1 and Q2 2024 Apple sales generated approximately $100 billion in cash proceeds and approximately $30+ billion in after-tax gain, contributing materially to Berkshire's record 2024 cash position of approximately $277 billion by end of Q2 and approximately $325 billion by end of Q3 2024. The Apple position remained Berkshire's largest common-equity holding despite the trim, ending Q2 2024 at approximately 400 million shares worth approximately $90 billion.

The Q2 2024 Apple sale triggered substantial market and analyst commentary on whether Buffett was signaling broader concern about U.S. large-cap equity valuations, the U.S. fiscal trajectory, or simply continuing the Q1 2024 tax-optimization program at larger scale. Buffett himself avoided confirming any of those interpretations in subsequent commentary, reiterating that Apple remained a wonderful business.

Buffett also disclosed in 2024 that Berkshire had paid $26.8 billion in U.S. corporate taxes in 2024 — more than any other U.S. corporation — partly as a result of the realized gains on the Apple sales. The 2024 shareholder letter is the primary source for the broader 2024 Apple-position and tax-rationale commentary.
